title: South Fork Well Depth and Drilling Cost
meta_description: South Fork wells have a 60-foot median depth, 13 gpm median yield, and typical finished costs of $9,000-$16,500.
h1: South Fork, Colorado Well Depth, Yield, and Cost
intro_html:
South Fork sits near Alpine and Gerrard in Rio Grande County, where well records show a wide range of drilling conditions. Among permitted wells within 5 miles, the median total depth is 60 feet, but the middle half runs from 44 to 202 feet. That spread matters when comparing a drilling estimate to nearby records.

Most permits are for domestic or household use. The records also point to two different water settings: many wells identify an unnamed or fractured-bedrock aquifer, while others draw from the unconfined San Luis Valley aquifer. Use these numbers as a planning guide, not as a guarantee for a particular lot.

sections.heading: How deep are wells around South Fork?
sections.html:
South Fork wells have a 60-foot median reported depth. The middle half of wells falls between 44 and 202 feet, so a bid near the shallow end may fit some sites while another lot can require substantially more drilling. The 90th-percentile depth is 400 feet, and the deepest record reaches 1,600 feet.

About 63% of wells are under 100 feet, while 20% are 100 to 300 feet. Another 14% fall between 300 and 600 feet, and 3% are deeper than 600 feet. For a buyer, the nearby well records are more useful than a countywide rule. Ground conditions, exact location, and the aquifer encountered can change the depth quickly, particularly where fractured bedrock is involved.

sections.heading: What water yield can a South Fork well make?
sections.html:
Reported well yields are generally favorable, but the records are incomplete: 549 wells report a pump yield. The median reported yield is 13.0 gallons per minute, with the middle half between 10.0 and 15.0 gallons per minute. About 46% of reported wells produce 15 or more gallons per minute, and 45% produce between 5 and 15 gallons per minute.

Low-yield wells still occur. The records show 7% between 1 and 5 gallons per minute and 2% under 1 gallon per minute. A result under 1 gallon per minute can limit household recovery and storage needs, even if the well is usable. Ask for the well test, production rate, pump setting, and storage arrangement rather than relying only on a neighbor's result.

sections.heading: What does the water table show near South Fork?
sections.html:
Static water level means the depth from the ground surface to the water when the well is not actively pumping. Among 159 records that report this measurement, the median is 30 feet, with the middle half between 12 and 86 feet. That is useful for estimating pumping conditions, but it is not the same as well depth or guaranteed drawdown during use.

The decade medians do not show a clear long-term decline in these records. Measurements were 28 feet below ground surface in the 2000s, 26 feet in the 2010s, and 30 feet in the 2020s. Those figures come from different wells and measurement dates, so they should not replace a current measurement at the property under contract.

sections.heading: South Fork permit history and local drillers
sections.html:
Colorado DWR records list 1,952 permitted wells within 5 miles of South Fork, with 1,391 recorded as constructed. Permit activity was strongest in the 1990s, with 461 permits, followed by 426 in the 2000s. The records include 180 permits in the 2020s, and the newest permit year is 2026.

The most active drillers in this local record are Valley Pump Company (Self, Clinton L.), with 373 wells; American Drilling Service (Dewberry, Bradford W.), with 239; and Irrigation Engineering & Supp. (Burk, Coy), with 107. These names help identify local history, but they do not guarantee availability, current licensing status, or suitability for a new site.

sections.heading: What does a new well cost near South Fork?
sections.html:
The cost model for South Fork assumes mixed sedimentary and alluvial ground. A typical drilling rate is $50 to $75 per foot. At the 60-foot median depth, the drilled hole works out to about $3,000 to $4,500.

A finished well is more than the drilled hole. Including the pump, tank, trenching, and electrical, the model estimates about $9,000 to $16,500 at the median depth. A deeper hole, difficult access, casing or grout requirements, and site-specific electrical or trenching work can move the actual bid. Get the estimate in writing and confirm which items are included, especially pump equipment, testing, permits, and connection to the house.

sections.heading: South Fork risks to check before building
sections.html:
Yield is the main uncertainty shown in the records. Most reported wells produce at least 5 gallons per minute, but 2% are under 1 gallon per minute and 7% are between 1 and 5 gallons per minute. Dry holes and poor production are possible, particularly where a site depends on a narrow fracture rather than a consistent water-bearing layer. A driller cannot promise that one nearby result will repeat on your lot.

There are 2 mapped PFAS sampling or contamination sites within about 10 miles. No historic mine features and no EPA Superfund or cleanup sites are mapped in that area. Test existing water before purchase and plan for a new-well water test after construction. Confirm septic setbacks, replacement-area needs, access for drilling equipment, and the legal well use with Colorado DWR before finalizing a building plan.

sections.heading: Buying or building on a South Fork lot
sections.html:
Start by pulling the DWR permit and construction records for the property and nearby wells. Compare reported depths, yields, static levels, aquifer names, and completion details, giving extra attention to Alpine, Gerrard, and the area immediately around the lot. A cluster of shallow wells can support a different expectation than an isolated deep or fractured-bedrock well.

Most local permits are for domestic or household use, but the allowed use of a particular permit controls what you can do. Exempt household-use wells are subject to Colorado rules, including the 35-gallon-per-minute pumping limit. In an over-appropriated basin, an augmentation plan may be required for some uses. Before closing, have a qualified well professional review the records, test the existing water, inspect the pump system, and price access, septic, and trenching together with the house site.

A finished well with pump, tank, trenching, and electrical is estimated at $9,000 to $16,500. Site access and deeper drilling can change the bid.

About 2% report under 1 gallon per minute, while 46% report 15 or more. Ask for a documented well test because nearby production does not guarantee the same result.

That does not establish water quality at a home. Test an existing well before buying and test a new well after construction for common contaminants and any concern identified by local conditions.
